CASE REPORT
A 48-year-old man with a history consistent with SPS
presented to the clinic. His previous history showed that he met
several diagnostic criteria for GAD( j) SPS and had a muscle
biopsy positive for myositis. He had been a self-employed car-
penter until his muscle spasticity was no longer able to be
controlled with diazepam (10 mg 4 times a day) and baclofen
(20 mg orally 4 times a day), thereby preventing him from
working. Adverse effects of these oral drugs prevented upward
titration of the medications. He was able to walk without an
assist device but used a cane for long walks. He reported jaw
stiffness that interfered with mouth opening and was starting to
interfere with speech and the ability to eat. The patient received
disability benefits because of his stiffness and pain. Medical
history also included occasional blurred vision and shortness of
breath, hypertension, Prinzmetal angina, and deep vein throm-
bosis requiring anticoagulation.
On physical examination, the patient was walking with-
out an assistive device. He had jaw tightness, deep tendon re-
flexes 1/4 in upper and lower extremities, decreased light-touch
sensation in left upper and lower extremities, and decreased
range of motion in cervical/lumbar spine. His Ashworth scores
were 3 to 4 (Table 1) in the upper and lower extremities.
Before intrathecal catheter placement, the patient was
given appropriate education and evaluation, informed consent
was obtained, and he was instructed to hold warfarin for 7 days
before the procedure. On the morning of the trial, coagulation
results were confirmed to be normal, and informed consent was
reviewed. Antispasmotic medications were held the morning of
catheter placement, and precatheter assessment was performed
by the physical therapist, and documentation of the modified
Ashworth scale was recorded in proximal and distal muscle
groups of the upper and lower extremities. After receiving 2 mg
midazolam, intravenously administered, with local anesthesia
and using strict aseptic technique, a low lumbar paramedian
approach (17 g Tuohy epidural needle; intrathecal trial catheter,
Medtronic, Minneapolis, Minnesota) was used to place a tem-
porary intrathecal catheter. It was advanced to the T1 level under
fluoroscopy and documented with radiographs. The T1 catheter
tip level was chosen in an attempt to obtain relief of upper-
extremity and shoulder symptoms. The intrathecal catheter trial
was performed with an initial bolus of baclofen 50 Kg followed
by gradual increase of 50 Kg/d, up to a maximum 150 Kg/d,
where maximal effect was seen. Evaluation of motor tone by our
physical therapist was performed 2 and 4 hours after initiation of
trial, and the next day. Functional assessments along with any
drug adverse effects were recorded by the physical therapist
(Table 2). Maximal improvement in spasticity was reached
24 hours following initial baclofen trial. The intrathecal catheter
was removed, and the patient then discharged home.
During intrathecal baclofen trial, the patient showed im-
provements in modified Ashworth scores with a decrease of up
to 3 points in the upper extremities and 2 points in the lower
extremities (Table 2). The Ashworth scores were 1 in the
proximal extremities and 2 in the distal extremities at an intra-

thecal baclofen infusion rate of 200 Kg/d with no negative ad-
verse effects. Approximately 2 weeks later, the patient was
admitted and implanted with a permanent intrathecal drug de-
livery system (Medtronic SynchroMed II). The starting dose of
baclofen of 100 Kg/d and Ashworth scores of 3/4 distal and 1/2
proximal were re-recorded with no reported adverse effects. The
initial intrathecal baclofen dose following pump placement is
lower than the final baclofen trial dose because the patient has
just received sedation for pump placement and to avoid initial
complications such as bladder/urinary retention. The intrathecal

baclofen dose was increased the following day to 150 Kg/d with
Ashworth scores of 2 distal and 1 proximal recorded with no
reported adverse effects. Over the next 6 months, intrathecal
baclofen was titrated to muscle tone and symptom control with
a final intrathecal infusion rate of 200 Kg/d. At this dose rate,
the patient reported some residual spasticity (muscle tone at
clinic visit reported as 1+), especially in the masseter and neck
muscles (sternocleidomastoid). This neck spasm was treated
with botulinum A toxin injections and diazepam with overall
improvement in symptoms. After an additional 6 months of
therapy, the intrathecal baclofen dose had been gradually ti-
trated upward to 1050 Kg/d. This dose has changed little in
recent months (12Y18 months after pump implant) with a slight
upward dose titration to the current 1200 Kg/d. The patient has
reported no other significant adverse effects and with overall
satisfaction in his intrathecal baclofen therapy.

The patient reported none of these adverse ef-
fects at 6-month follow-up, although he did receive botulinum
toxin A injections for stiffness in his neck and jaw.

Our
patient completed a 4-day trial of intrathecal baclofen titrated to
effect before pump implantation. It is possible that continuous
intrathecal trialing, as opposed to single-injection technique,
allowed a better determination of the effective therapeutic dose
and ensure posttrialing successful therapy.
